claims.claim: As of June 30, 2018, state and local governments in the United States operated 17,541 law enforcement agencies that employed at least one full-time-equivalent sworn officer with general arrest powers; those agencies employed 1,214,000 full-time personnel, of whom 788,000 (65%) were sworn and 427,000 (35%) were civilian.

The 2018 census breaks the 17,541 agencies down as 11,824 local police departments (67%), 3,051 sheriffs' offices (17%), 1,753 special jurisdiction agencies (10%), 647 constable or marshal offices (4%), 217 tribal agencies (1%), and 49 primary state law enforcement agencies (0.3%).

Most U.S. policing agencies are small: in 2018, 7,055 agencies employing fewer than 10 full-time-equivalent sworn officers made up 40% of all state and local agencies, while the 80 agencies with 1,000 or more FTE sworn officers were 0.5% of agencies but employed 29% (228,000) of all full-time sworn personnel.

Federal law enforcement is a separate and much smaller layer: in fiscal year 2020, 90 federal agencies employed 136,815 full-time officers authorized to make arrests and carry firearms, with the Department of Homeland Security and its Office of Inspector General accounting for 49% (66,410) of them.

Sheriffs' offices are county-level agencies distinguished by their custodial and court-related duties; BJS's general-purpose agency counts exclude sheriffs' offices with only jail and court duties, and BJS defines a jail as a facility generally operated under the authority of a sheriff, police chief, or county or city administrator.

The United States has a dual court structure: Congress has established 13 U.S. Courts of Appeals and 94 U.S. District Courts beneath the Supreme Court created by Article III, while each state maintains its own trial courts, often intermediate appellate courts, and a court of last resort; state courts handle most criminal cases and are the final arbiters of state law.

Charging discretion rests with the prosecutor. In Bordenkircher v. Hayes (1978) the Supreme Court stated that so long as the prosecutor has probable cause to believe the accused committed a statutory offense, the decision whether to prosecute and what charge to file generally rests entirely in the prosecutor's discretion, subject to the limit that selection may not be deliberately based on an unjustifiable standard such as race or religion.

Prosecutors are executive-branch officials rather than court personnel. BJS describes state court prosecutors as serving in the executive branch of state government, afforded broad discretion by law in determining who is charged and whether a case goes to trial, with the chief prosecutor - district attorney, county attorney, commonwealth attorney, or state's attorney - answerable to the public as an elected or appointed official; BJS's 2007 national census counted 2,330 state prosecutors' offices.

In some states the county's principal criminal justice officers hold office by constitutional command: article XI, section 1(b) of the California Constitution requires the Legislature to provide for an elected county sheriff and an elected district attorney in each county. Arrangements of this kind vary from state to state.

Convictions come overwhelmingly from guilty pleas rather than trials. In federal court in fiscal year 2025, of 66,662 individuals sentenced, 97.7% (65,099) pleaded guilty and 2.3% (1,563) were convicted at trial.

The Supreme Court in Missouri v. Frye (2012), citing Bureau of Justice Statistics data, stated that ninety-seven percent of federal convictions and ninety-four percent of state convictions are the result of guilty pleas. The state figure rests on BJS felony sentencing data from 2006 and has no comparable annual national update, so it must be dated rather than presented as current.

Jails are local, short-term, and mostly pretrial: BJS defines a jail as holding individuals before and after arraignment, usually beyond 72 hours, and those sentenced to incarceration of 1 year or less. At midyear 2023 local jails held 664,200 people, of whom 70% (467,600) were unconvicted and 30% (196,600) were convicted; from July 2022 to June 2023, people spent an average of 32 days in custody before release.

Prisons are state or federal and hold longer sentences: BJS defines a prison as a long-term facility run by a state or the federal government, typically holding people with sentences of more than 1 year, with sentence length varying by state. At yearend 2023, 1,254,224 people were under state or federal prison jurisdiction - 1,097,597 under state authority and 156,627 under the Federal Bureau of Prisons - and 96% (1,210,300) were sentenced to more than 1 year.

Community corrections supervises far more people than institutions confine: at yearend 2023, of about 5,530,300 people under adult correctional supervision, 3,772,000 were on probation (3,103,400) or parole (680,400) in the community while 1,852,900 were incarcerated in prisons or local jails - roughly two people supervised in the community for every one confined.

There is no single U.S. criminal justice system. BJS describes many similar but individually unique systems, says the response to crime is mainly a state and local function, and documents discretion at every stage: police deciding whether to investigate or arrest, prosecutors whether to file charges, judges on bail and sentence, correctional officials on custody decisions, and paroling authorities on release dates and conditions, with the limits of that discretion varying by jurisdiction.

Six states - Alaska, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Rhode Island, and Vermont - operate integrated systems that combine prisons and jails, so their entire confined population is counted in BJS prison statistics rather than split between jail and prison series.

Jails are administered by roughly 2,848 local jail jurisdictions nationwide, the frame from which BJS drew its 2023 Annual Survey of Jails sample, covering the 45 states that do not operate integrated jail-prison systems.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The commonly repeated figure of 'about 18,000 police agencies' in the United States.
positions: Textbooks and press accounts routinely state that the United States has roughly 18,000 law enforcement agencies, usually without a date.
The most recent BJS census counted 17,541 state and local agencies employing at least one full-time-equivalent sworn officer as of June 30, 2018, down 444 (2%) from 2008.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson gives the BJS number with its reference date and notes explicitly that 18,000 is a rounded approximation of a census figure, not a live count. The 2018 census is the most recent in the series; the sampling frame it was drawn from listed 19,091 agencies before eligibility screening, which is one reason higher round numbers circulate.

conflictingEvidence.issue: What share of convictions comes from guilty pleas, and whether a single number covers both state and federal courts.
positions: Missouri v. Frye (2012) states 97% of federal and 94% of state convictions result from guilty pleas, citing BJS sources including 2006 state felony sentencing data.
The U.S. Sentencing Commission reports a current federal figure each fiscal year: 97.7% of individuals sentenced in FY2025 pleaded guilty.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the USSC FY2025 figure as the current, dated federal number and attributes the state figure to the Frye opinion with its 2012 date and older underlying data, stating plainly that no comparable annual national series exists for state courts. It does not present a single blended percentage.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Total correctional population at yearend 2023: whether to add the component counts.
positions: Adding community supervision (3,772,000) and incarcerated (1,852,900) gives 5,624,900.
BJS reports a total correctional population of 5,530,300, which adjusts for people counted in more than one status.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses BJS's published total of 5,530,300 and does not sum the components, because the components overlap (people on parole who are also on probation, people on supervision held in a jail or prison).

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft asserted that 'Police, Courts, And Corrections is a foundational concept in Criminal Justice & Criminology' and treated the phrase as a single concept to be defined. Research does not support treating it as one concept; it names three separately constituted sets of institutions.

The draft's claim that the topic is 'a concept students use to organize information, ask better questions, and explain relationships' is content-free boilerplate with no factual referent and no source.
The draft's analogy ('a label on a toolbox drawer', 'reading a map legend') carried no institutional content and asserted nothing verifiable.
The draft's vocabulary entries ('context', 'evidence', 'application') were generic study-skills terms unrelated to the criminal justice institutions this topic covers.
The draft's worked example described a student reading a scenario rather than a case moving through the three components.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the entire generated draft: every field except the curriculum coordinates and the title was rewritten from verified sources.
Anchored every count and proportion to a named BJS, USSC, or Administrative Office publication with its reference date, per the subject's caution that crime and justice statistics must be dated.
Used BJS's published total correctional population (5,530,300) rather than summing components, avoiding double-counting.
Stated the policing agency count as 17,541 as of June 30, 2018 rather than the undated 'about 18,000' in general circulation, and explained the discrepancy.
Separated the current federal guilty-plea figure (USSC FY2025) from the older state figure quoted in Missouri v. Frye, rather than presenting one number for both systems.

Attributed prosecutorial charging discretion to Bordenkircher v. Hayes (1978) as primary authority rather than to a secondary summary, and included the opinion's stated limit on selective prosecution.

Added an explicit statement of U.S. jurisdiction, an explicit note that state law and state institutional arrangements vary, and an explicit educational-material statement, per the subject's legal-review profile.

Removed two sentences drafted from general knowledge that the research had not verified - a blanket assertion that sheriffs and prosecutors are elected countywide, and a description of how probation agencies are administered. The prosecutor point was replaced with BJS's own formulation (executive branch, elected or appointed) and one verified state example from the California Constitution; the probation-administration point was cut entirely and left to corrections:probation-and-parole.

Named the downstream topics that own each area in depth so this lesson stays a map rather than duplicating court-structure, arrest-through-trial, plea-bargaining, jails-versus-prisons, probation-and-parole, or the policing unit.
rightsIssues: All sources are U.S. federal government publications or U.S. Supreme Court opinions. None of the agency sites carries an explicit reuse license on the pages consulted, so agency publications are recorded as REFERENCE_ONLY and no agency prose was adapted; all lesson prose is original synthesis.

The two Supreme Court opinions are recorded as PUBLIC_DOMAIN because U.S. judicial opinions are not subject to copyright as a matter of settled law, not by inference from the hosting domain. Two short quoted phrases from Bordenkircher v. Hayes appear in the lesson with express attribution to the opinion.

No robots.txt or terms page on bjs.ojp.gov, www.uscourts.gov, or www.ussc.gov states an AI-ingestion permission, so aiIngestionAllowed is recorded as false throughout; the checks were performed on 2026-08-18.

The Missouri v. Frye and Bordenkircher v. Hayes texts were read from the Library of Congress United States Reports scans because supremecourt.gov returned HTTP 404 to the fetcher. The Census of State and Local Law Enforcement Agencies, Sheriffs' Offices, Jail Inmates, Prisoners, and Correctional Populations reports were read as the BJS-hosted PDFs; the landing pages are given as the citable URLs.

sourceRecords.title: Census of State and Local Law Enforcement Agencies, 2018 - Statistical Tables (NCJ 302187)
sourceRecords.provider: Bureau of Justice Statistics, U.S. Department of Justice
sourceRecords.notes: The authoritative national count of state and local law enforcement agencies. Read the full PDF (28 pages) for the June 30, 2018 reference date, the 17,541 agency total, Table 1's agency-type breakdown, the 1,214,000 full-time personnel split into 788,000 sworn and 427,000 civilian, the 7,055 agencies with fewer than 10 FTE sworn officers (40% of agencies), and the 80 agencies with 1,000 or more FTE sworn officers (0.5% of agencies, 29% of sworn personnel). Supports the fragmentation and size-distribution claims. No source wording reused.

sourceRecords.title: Federal Law Enforcement Officers, 2020 - Statistical Tables (NCJ 304752)
sourceRecords.provider: Bureau of Justice Statistics, U.S. Department of Justice
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the federal law enforcement layer: 136,815 full-time officers with arrest and firearm authority across 90 agencies in fiscal year 2020, with DHS and its Office of Inspector General accounting for 49% (66,410). Used only to size the federal layer against the state and local one; the lesson does not describe individual federal agencies' jurisdictions.

sourceRecords.title: Sheriffs' Offices, 2016: Personnel (NCJ 252834)
sourceRecords.provider: Bureau of Justice Statistics, U.S. Department of Justice
sourceRecords.notes: Read the full bulletin PDF. Supports two points: sheriffs' offices made up 20% (3,012) of the 15,322 general-purpose agencies and employed 25% (173,000) of their 701,000 full-time sworn officers as of June 30, 2016; and BJS's definition of general-purpose agencies expressly excludes sheriffs' offices with only jail and court duties, which establishes that some sheriffs' offices are custodial and court-serving rather than patrol agencies.

sourceRecords.title: Comparing Federal and State Courts
sourceRecords.provider: Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the dual court structure: 13 U.S. Courts of Appeals and 94 U.S. District Courts established by Congress beneath the Article III Supreme Court, and state systems with a court of last resort, sometimes intermediate appellate courts, and trial courts. Also supports that state courts hear most criminal cases and are the final arbiters of state law. Used for structure only; courts:court-structure covers jurisdiction and hierarchy in depth.

sourceRecords.title: Prosecutors in State Courts, 2007 - Statistical Tables (NCJ 234211)
sourceRecords.provider: Bureau of Justice Statistics, U.S. Department of Justice
sourceRecords.notes: Read the PDF directly (12 pages, published December 2011); this is the URL that resolved, and it is the most recent BJS national census of state court prosecutors. Supports the structural claims only: prosecutors serve in the executive branch of state government, are afforded broad discretion by law over who is charged and whether a case goes to trial, and the chief prosecutor is answerable to the public as an elected or appointed official under titles that vary by state. The 2,330 office count is given in the lesson with its 2007 date. The report's caseload and budget figures are too old to present as current and are not used.

sourceRecords.title: California Constitution, Article XI, Section 1
sourceRecords.provider: California Legislative Counsel (official California Legislative Information)
sourceRecords.license: California statutory and constitutional text published by the Legislative Counsel is not subject to copyright restriction on reproduction of the text itself
sourceRecords.notes: Read the official text. Subdivision (b) requires the Legislature to provide for county powers, an elected county sheriff, an elected district attorney, an elected assessor, and an elected governing body in each county. Used as one verified state example so the lesson can illustrate county-level electoral accountability without generalizing to all fifty states, which the research did not check. No constitutional text is quoted in the lesson.

sourceRecords.title: Sourcebook of Federal Sentencing Statistics, Fiscal Year 2025, Table 12: Guilty Pleas and Trials by Type of Crime
sourceRecords.notes: The current, dated federal guilty-plea figure. Read the table PDF directly: of 66,662 individuals sentenced in fiscal year 2025, 65,099 (97.7%) pleaded guilty and 1,563 (2.3%) were convicted at trial. The table's per-offense rows also show the range - immigration 99.7% plea, murder 74.8% plea - which the lesson uses to note that the plea share is not uniform across offense types. The Sourcebook landing page is at https://www.ussc.gov/research/sourcebook-2025.

sourceRecords.title: Missouri v. Frye, 566 U.S. 134 (2012)
sourceRecords.provider: Supreme Court of the United States (United States Reports, via the Library of Congress)
sourceRecords.license: U.S. judicial opinions are not subject to copyright

sourceRecords.license: U.S. judicial opinions are not subject to copyright

sourceRecords.title: Jail Inmates in 2023 - Statistical Tables (NCJ 309965)
sourceRecords.provider: Bureau of Justice Statistics, U.S. Department of Justice
sourceRecords.notes: Read the full PDF (35 pages, published April 2025). Supports the jail figures and definitions: 664,200 people in local jail custody at midyear 2023; 70% (467,600) unconvicted and 30% (196,600) convicted; average 32 days in custody before release from July 2022 to June 2023; the BJS definition of a jail as a facility generally operated under the authority of a sheriff, police chief, or county or city administrator, holding people before and after arraignment usually beyond 72 hours and those sentenced to 1 year or less; the 2,848 jail jurisdictions in the 2023 Annual Survey of Jails frame; and the exclusion of the six combined jail-prison states.

sourceRecords.title: Prisoners in 2023 - Statistical Tables (NCJ 310197)
sourceRecords.provider: Bureau of Justice Statistics, U.S. Department of Justice
sourceRecords.notes: Read the full PDF (47 pages, published September 2025). Supports the prison figures and definitions: 1,254,224 people under state or federal prison jurisdiction at yearend 2023, of whom Table 2 gives 1,097,597 state and 156,627 federal; 96% (1,210,300) sentenced to more than 1 year; the BJS definition of a prison as a long-term facility run by a state or the federal government typically holding people with sentences of more than 1 year, with sentence length varying by state; and the list of six states operating integrated prison-jail systems.

sourceRecords.title: Correctional Populations in the United States, 2023 - Statistical Tables (NCJ 310413)
sourceRecords.provider: Bureau of Justice Statistics, U.S. Department of Justice
sourceRecords.notes: Read the full PDF (26 pages, published September 2025). The single source that lets institutional and community corrections be compared on the same basis at yearend 2023: total under correctional supervision 5,530,300 (BJS's published total, which adjusts for overlap between statuses); 3,772,000 under community supervision, comprising 3,103,400 on probation and 680,400 on parole; 1,852,900 incarcerated in prisons or local jails; a supervision rate of 2,100 per 100,000 adult residents, or 1 in 48 adults.

sourceRecords.title: The Justice System
sourceRecords.provider: Bureau of Justice Statistics, U.S. Department of Justice
sourceRecords.notes: BJS's own description of case flow. Supports two claims the lesson makes: that there is no single U.S. criminal justice system but many similar, individually unique ones, with the response to crime mainly a state and local function; and that discretion operates at every stage, with police, prosecutors, judges, correctional officials, and paroling authorities each holding a distinct decision, subject to limits that vary by jurisdiction. Used for the handoff and discretion structure only - criminal-justice-system:what-is-criminal-justice owns the system framing and the attrition funnel.
